title: Student notes on Schreiber Game Balance course ch3 Transitive Mechanics and Cost Curves (2011 blog)
label: practitioner
claim: Secondhand notes of Schreiber's Summer 2010 course. Transitive = some options flat-out better, balanced by cost; intransitive = no single best (RPS). Cost curve can be increasing, linear or decreasing; increasing favours long games, decreasing favours early game; right shape depends on expected game length. Choice between X and Y should cost more than X and Y separately. Too weak preferable to too strong. In persistent games power creep pushes cost curve up; raise very slowly. Polynomial not discussed.

title: Schreiber, Game Balance Concepts: Level 3 Transitive Mechanics and Cost Curves (primary)
label: practitioner
claim: Via fetch-summary: linear cost/benefit (+1 cost = +1 benefit) is 'pretty rare'; increasing curves (triangular or exponential) mean twice as good costs considerably more than twice as much; decreasing curves exist where hoarding has an opportunity cost, so twice the cost must be more than twice as good; custom curves exist. 'over time, the power level of the cost curve increases'; players may leave if they sense designer purposefully raises power to force purchases. Polynomial and supply/demand not mentioned. Quotes are from the summarizer, not checked against bytes.

title: Sirlin, Balancing Multiplayer Games Part 2: Viable Options
label: practitioner
claim: Balance has two sub-concepts: viable options and fairness. Dominant move = 'a move that is strictly better than any other you could do', 'the worst thing you can have in a competitive multiplayer game', probably has no real counter. Fairness = 'overall chance of winning, given different starting options', a global measure; local situations need not be fair. MvC2 has 54 characters, 'I'll say 10' viable in tournament, 'being generous'. Fighting-game context.

title: Sirlin, Balancing Multiplayer Games Part 1: Definitions
label: practitioner
claim: Balanced = 'a reasonably large number of options available to the player are viable'. Non-viable options 'just get in the way', adding complexity that makes a game harder to learn yet no more interesting. Tiers not discussed on this page (my earlier assumption was wrong).

title: Riot, /dev: Balance Framework Update (2020)
label: developer
claim: Riot: early on 'we ended up buffing slightly more often than nerfing'; after Worlds 2019 a spike of buff-heavy patches. Safeguard: if over half of balance changes in later patches are buffs, also explore nerfing top champions. Nerf flag if overperforming in ANY of four audience groups; buff only if underperforming in ALL four. Estimated win-rate changes are now compared with actual post-patch win rates. Patch 10.12 share of champions above underpowered metric: Average 81%, Skilled 87%, Elite 30%, Pro 36%, Solo Queue 93%, All 98%. Riot self-reports fewer threshold breaches in 2020 than 2019; no outside check.

title: How Slay the Spire's devs use data to balance (Game Developer, GDC 2019 coverage)

title: Castronova, On Virtual Economies (CESifo WP 752, 2002)
label: research

Footnote summarizing his 2001 study: pseudo-GDP of Norrath 'as much as $2,000 per capita annually'. Goods are digital, so 'costlessly created and destroyed': price ceilings create no excess demand, price floors no excess supply; government can peg prices. Lack of work, not work, causes disutility in an avatar economy. Per-hour wage, exchange-rate figures were NOT found in this paper (they are from the 2001 report, seen only in search snippets).

title: Dormans, Engineering Emergence (PhD thesis, UvA, 2012)
label: research
claim: Downloaded and grepped, not read end to end. Positive feedback amplifies small differences (Monopoly: early lucky break compounds); negative feedback diminishes differences (rubber-banding). Games have many positive loops because players do not want a game that is stable and drags on forever; games with only positive feedback seem too random to many players. Sources create resources, drains destroy, converters swap, traders exchange. Static friction (fixed drain) vs dynamic friction (drain scales with energy, upgrades or progress) counter engine growth; dynamic adds a negative loop. Artificial players over thousands of runs can identify dominant strategies. Stated limits: internal-economy modelling suits board, strategy and management games; abstract-economy games like Chess and Go are hard to scope; progression mechanics get a separate chapter. Randomness lessens the chance of a dominant long- vs short-term investment strategy.
